$comment: The platform-suite registry (engineering/development.md § Platform suites). One entry per check that must run on a real macOS or Windows runner. `os`: runner labels (macos-26, windows-2025). `paths`: globs; a PR that touches one runs the suite, and the nightly and a manual dispatch run every suite. `on_pull_request`: false runs the suite nightly and on dispatch only, never on a pull request (the iOS Simulator suites, 2026-10-29: 49 PR jobs and about 820 macOS minutes in the 100 PR runs from 2026-10-28T10:50Z to 2026-10-29T02:25Z, 27 of them not green, gating nothing). `run`: the command, from the repo root after `npm ci` and `npm run build`. `why`: what this suite proves that Linux cannot. `docs_site`: true when the suite serves the built docs site; the workflow's `docs-site` job builds it once on Linux and the suite's job downloads it. tools/check-ownership.js (checkPlatformSuites) fails on a malformed entry or a `run` that names a file that is gone.

suites.name: export-confine
suites.why: A render reads a local file only by REAL path inside the deck folder (media note §4.11). macOS reaches /tmp and $TMPDIR through symlinks (/private/tmp, /private/var), the case a real-path check gets wrong first; Linux cannot show it. The Mermaid worker's own page applies the same check. Windows runs as export-confine-windows.

suites.name: export-confine-windows
suites.why: The same CLI confinement checks as export-confine, on Windows: the CLI names its output page with pathToFileURL (file:///C:/…), and file-confine must turn that back into a path on the same drive and refuse a host-qualified (UNC) address. It uses the full `npm run build` (build-windows proves that build passes there). Symlink creation may need a privilege the runner lacks; if so those tests fail with EPERM and the run shows it.

suites.name: wait-for-macos
suites.run: for t in timeout gtimeout flock perl; do command -v $t || echo "no $t"; done; brew install coreutils && node --test test/unit/tools/wait-for.test.js test/unit/tools/warn-unbounded-wait.test.js
suites.why: tools/wait-for.sh takes its lock with flock(1) or, where that is missing, perl's flock builtin, and needs GNU timeout (gtimeout on macOS). macOS ships neither flock(1) nor timeout, so the perl path and the exit-69 'missing dependency' path are the ones a Mac takes; Linux tests drive them only by pinning WAIT_FOR_LOCK_IMPL and a controlled PATH (engineering/development.md § Waiting for a slow job: 'macOS itself remains UNVERIFIED'). The first two runs (jobs 117883739691, 117885882571) showed a stock macOS runner has perl but no timeout, gtimeout or flock; the tests failed because their lock probe called flock(1), not because wait-for.sh did (its own run-mode test passed). The probe now falls back to perl, `isLive` to `ps` (no /proc), and the entry installs coreutils first (the supported state).

suites.name: build-windows
suites.why: `npm run build` runs tools/check-ownership.js first, and on Windows every gate that compared a backslash path with a forward-slash allowlist reported its sanctions stale and aborted the build (platform-suites run 39197530212, job 117883739719), so no CLI suite could use the full build there; the path, Biome-launch, command-length and report-path fixes in tools/check-ownership.js and tools/check-lint-coverage.js removed that. The suite's own build step IS the check (the default `npm run build`); `run` then re-runs the ownership gate and confirms the generated artifacts exist.

suites.name: os-sandbox-measure
suites.why: The code door reads the OS sandbox layer before it runs a stranger's code, and an npm plugin runs only where it reads `on` (threat-model note §6 decisions 7 and 13). macOS (sandbox_check) and Windows (chrome://sandbox) are read differently from Linux, and only a real runner of each starts Chromium's sandbox to be read. The npm admission test then runs the real door there: an npm plugin draws exactly when the measured layer admits it.

suites.name: ios-safari-studio-ipad
suites.why: Real Mobile Safari, in an iPad iOS Simulator, drives the Studio preview with a quoted-attribute payload and the nested-form mXSS shape through the first write and the patch path (#2899), and proves its own detector fires. Playwright's WebKit on Linux is not iOS Safari, and nothing else in CI reaches it. A simulator runs on the Mac's hardware, so it is not a physical device. One device per job: the iPad and the iPhone back to back took 21 to 27 of the job's 30 minutes on main and were canceled at 30 on slower runners with every check passed (runs 43278314890, 43285290891; flaky shape F4), most of it two simulator boots in series, so each device now has the whole limit, as the undo suites do.

Playwright's WebKit on Linux is not iOS Safari, and nothing else in CI reaches it. A simulator runs on the Mac's hardware, so it is not a physical device. One device per job: the iPad and the iPhone back to back took 21 to 27 of the job's 30 minutes on main and were canceled at 30 on slower runners with every check passed (runs 43278314890, 43285290891; flaky shape F4), most of it two simulator boots in series, so each device now has the whole limit, as the undo suites do.

suites.name: ios-safari-player-charts-ipad
suites.why: Chart detail cards in an exported HTML player, in real Mobile Safari in an iPad iOS Simulator (player-charts.mjs, #3259). The real CLI exports two decks; WebDriver touches tap a funnel band and the card must pin there, sit in the top layer inside the visible viewport and never under the finger, take touches, close on a second tap or a tap elsewhere, and never turn the slide; a deck whose detail carries author styles must keep them inside the card (HARD RULE #22). A touch log records where each tap landed, so a missed tap and a card that did not open read differently. docs/e2e/player-chart-reveal.spec.ts proves the same in Playwright's WebKit on Linux, which is not iOS Safari. One device per job, as the Studio suites run.

suites.name: ios-safari-font-cache
suites.why: Whether real Mobile Safari, in an iPad and an iPhone iOS Simulator, reads the Studio's warmed fonts from its HTTP cache (studio-warm.ts fetches 31 faces, about 2.7 MB, after the first slide; #3087). The server counts what reaches it: after the warm-up, an edit that adds an emoji, a code block and `finish: sketch` must send no font request; a control arm, on its own origin and identical except that the font files are sent `no-store`, must send some, so the probe can see a miss. Chromium, Firefox and Linux WebKit were checked on Linux; Safari was not, and a miss there downloads those 2.7 MB twice on every iPhone visit. The service worker is kept out, as it was for those engines: its Cache Storage path is a separate question.

suites.name: ios-safari-photo-memory-ipad
suites.why: Measures what ten 12MP photos cost real Mobile Safari, in an iPad iOS Simulator, shown by their own addresses and through the Studio's preview-sized copies (docs/src/lib/preview-image-scale.ts, #2998): the physical footprint of the simulator's WebKit processes, read on the Mac with vmmap. It fails when the originals cost under 60 MB (the reader is not reading Safari) or the copies cost more than 60% of them; CI has read 86 to 117 MB against 17 to 34 MB. It was part of ios-safari-studio until it took that job to 27.6 of its 30 minutes. A simulator has no memory limit, so it shows the cost, not the tab reload. One device per job (DEVICES), as the undo and Studio suites run: in the 14 nightlies to 2026-11-20 the two-device ios-safari-photo-memory job was cancelled at its 30-minute limit once with no test failed, so each device now has the whole limit.

suites.name: ios-safari-present-memory
suites.why: What Present costs real Mobile Safari, in an iPhone iOS Simulator, on a deck of eighteen phone photos imported through "Import deck…" (present-memory.mjs, 24 MB; the owner's deck was 33 MB of data: text and reloaded the tab on an iPhone before #3148). It opens Present, steps six slides, times each until the next slide shows and its photo decodes, and reads the simulator's WebKit footprint with vmmap before and after. It fails when a step's photo does not decode, the page reloads, or Present adds more than PRESENT_MEMORY_CAP_MB (300; the first run read 795 MB on main and 124 MB after #3148). Times are reported, never judged (HARD RULE #32). The production site runs as a second arm that is reported, not judged, and time-boxed: the before until #3148 deployed, the live site after. A simulator has no memory limit, so it shows the cost, not the reload.

suites.name: ios-safari-present-narration
suites.why: What Present with narration costs real Mobile Safari, in an iPhone iOS Simulator. The owner's iPhone reloaded the tab when Present played a 4K deck with narration and Guide on, and not with narration off (2026-11-17). present-narration.mjs builds a 30-slide 4K deck with an @say note on every slide (about ten minutes of narration); the probe imports it, installs a stand-in for the owner's voice, Gemini 3.1 Flash TTS through OpenRouter (the reload happens with it and not with Kokoro), answered in the page as OpenRouter answers it: headerless PCM of a sentence's length (no key spent, HARD RULE #24; NARRATION_VOICE picks Kokoro or Gemini's own API instead), and opens Present with Guide on. On the simulator no WebDriver press reaches the page, so only a script click starts Present and iOS keeps audio suspended; the probe therefore walks the deck with Next every 10 s, as a presenter would, so each slide's narration is still requested and cached: voice on until Present reaches slide 15 (judged on that work, with 10 minutes only as a ceiling); a voice-off arm runs only when NARRATION_SILENT_S is set. Every 30 s it reads the slide, the narration audio the page has decoded, and the simulator's WebKit footprint with vmmap. It fails when the voice arm stops before slide 15 or asks for under four sentences a slide, the page reloads, no audio was decoded or the decoded audio passes NARRATION_AUDIO_CAP_MB (40), the footprint reader reads under 50 MB before Present, or the footprint grows past NARRATION_MEMORY_CAP_MB (300). A simulator has no memory limit, so it shows the cost, not the reload.

suites.name: ios-safari-present-keepalive
suites.why: What keeps a playing deck playing on an iPhone, in real Mobile Safari in an iPhone iOS Simulator (present-keepalive-probe.js, #3333). Present must hold a screen wake lock (published as data-wake); Fullscreen, which iPhone Safari cannot grant, must turn on the immersive layout and its chrome must fade; a real WebDriver touch tap on the slide must bring the chrome back; Play must put the captions inside the slide with a moving highlight; Next while playing must play the next slide on its own with the lock still held; closing must stop the narration. Playwright's WebKit on Linux is not iOS Safari: it sends a tap as a bare click, and the first tap rule passed Chromium and failed there. The checks judge states reached, never durations (HARD RULE #32). A simulator does not auto-lock, so this proves the lock is granted and held, not that a real screen stays awake.

suites.name: ios-safari-undo-ipad
suites.why: Filo's undo in real Safari, on one device per job: Mobile Safari in an iPad iOS Simulator. One job ran all three devices back to back and took 25.4 of its 30 minutes, passing only on a fast runner (flaky shape F4); a device is about 3 minutes of probe plus its simulator's boot, so each now has the whole limit. It runs WebKit's own undo and redo commands (what Safari's Edit menu, the iOS shake, the three-finger swipe and the iPad keyboard bar send, as a historyUndo beforeinput), taps the Studio's Undo and Redo where it draws them, then reloads and undoes the edit made before the reload; on the Mac a real ⌘Z key does it too. Playwright's WebKit on Linux is not Safari. A simulator cannot shake or take an IME composition, so the gestures themselves and Japanese input stay a person's check (PR #2959 P3).

suites.name: ios-safari-chat-storage-ipad
suites.why: Studio chats in real Mobile Safari, in an iPad iOS Simulator (#3138, engineering/decisions/2026-11-11-studio-storage-pointer-records.md §11): threads an earlier build left in localStorage move to IndexedDB across a real reload, whole, including a deck never opened, and the localStorage allowance is what local-quota.ts assumes for WebKit (about 5.24 M Latin-1 characters, half once a value is non-Latin-1), which the fill warning's arithmetic rests on. Playwright's WebKit on Linux is not iOS Safari. Nightly and on dispatch only (on_pull_request false, the owner's call on #3138): no per-PR macOS job. suites.name: ios-safari-jpeg-ipad
suites.why: Every export JPEG goes through the shared encoder (docs/src/lib/lastra/jpeg.ts, `@laticent/lastra`) because the platforms' own encoders differ: a picture PowerPoint was 43.3 MB from an iPhone where Chromium wrote 12.5 MB. Linux WebKit uses libjpeg-turbo, like Chromium, so it cannot show what Apple's encoder writes. This runs the encoder in real Mobile Safari (an iPad iOS Simulator): its bytes must equal Node's and its luma stay above 38 dB; the step summary records Safari's own size and color sampling beside ours for a slide-sized synthetic photograph and four committed screenshots. A simulator runs on the Mac's CPU, so its timings are not a phone's. One device per job (DEVICES), as the undo and Studio suites run: in the 14 nightlies to 2026-11-20 the two-device ios-safari-jpeg job was cancelled at its 30-minute limit 3 times with no test failed, so each device now has the whole limit.

suites.name: ios-safari-focus-sync
suites.why: A click on a line in the Playground editor must center its slide in the preview and leave the editor where it is. The sync once judged its own preview scroll by time since the write, so a busy page delivered the event after the 120 ms echo window and the editor jumped 136 px (followup 2937-p2). Linux WebKit showed it only under CPU load and is not iOS Safari. This taps the editor 40 times in real Mobile Safari on an iPad Pro iOS Simulator, with the page kept busy on purpose, and fails if any tap moves the editor 2 px or more. The same probe fails 39 of 40 taps on the old code in Playwright's WebKit, so it can fail. A simulator runs on the Mac's CPU, so it is not a physical device. The iPhone is not run: a phone is never wide enough for the two-pane layout.

suites.name: office-quicklook
suites.run: node tools/office-quicklook.mjs --custgeom-only examples/inline-icons.md test/integration/baseline-decks/gallery.md && PROBE=office bash docs/scripts/ios-safari/run.sh
suites.why: iPhone Preview opens a .pptx with Apple's own Office importer, which draws it unlike PowerPoint, LibreOffice or Google Slides (it ignores embedded fonts, and collapsed every icon shape inside a group to a speck). macOS Quick Look uses the same importer; Linux has nothing that does. Renders each slide to a PNG under platform-suite-artifacts/office-quicklook/, as exported and as rewritten variants, so the comparison is seen without a phone.

suites.name: dead-code-windows
suites.run: node tools/quality-assessment.js --check --only dead-code && node --test test/unit/tools/quality-dead-code.test.js && p=tools/lib/zz-dead-probe && echo 'module.exports = 1;' > "$p.js" && ! node tools/quality-assessment.js --check --only dead-code && rm "$p.js"
suites.why: The dead-code pre-push job (owner's D1) runs on every contributor's machine. It starts knip through node (process.execPath plus node_modules/knip/bin/knip.js) because Windows cannot spawn the extensionless node_modules/.bin shim without a shell. This proves on a real Windows runner that the check runs and passes on the tree, that its unit tests pass, and, with a planted unused file, that it fails.

suites.name: pdf-pdfkit
suites.why: Apple PDFKit draws every PDF opened in Preview or on an iPhone, the owner's viewer, and Linux has nothing that runs it. The shared PDF writer draws a finish's backdrop with an image soft mask, a /Interpolate picture and paths (engineering/decisions/2026-11-20-backdrop-gradient-fidelity.md); this draws the demo deck's PDF through PDFKit, and a control with the backdrop photographed whole as before, and fails when any 32 px tile of the drawn page is more than 8 levels further from Chrome's screen than the control's: the mark of a dropped mask or a missing fade. PDFKit's own text rendering is in both and cancels. Pages and report under platform-suite-artifacts/pdf-pdfkit/.

suites.name: docs-scrollbars-windows
suites.run: cd docs && npm ci && npx playwright install chromium firefox && E2E_PREBUILT=1 E2E_RECORD=off npx playwright test e2e/scrollbar-width.spec.ts e2e/wheel-sideways.spec.ts --project=desktop --project=gecko --trace off
suites.why: Windows draws CLASSIC scrollbars that take layout space, which is where the owner saw inner panes keep the thick OS default (15-17px) because `scrollbar-width` is not inherited (#3345). scrollbar-width.spec.ts measures the Compose pane's bar against an `auto` control in Chromium and in a HEADED Firefox (Playwright's headless Firefox reports `scrollbar-width: none` for every element; Linux has no display for it, and its GTK bars are overlay anyway) and writes the widths to platform-suite-artifacts/. wheel-sideways.spec.ts checks a mouse wheel scrolls the slide pills and the slide map sideways, the owner's Windows report. Added at the owner's request (2026-11-21, "raise it") to verify on the platform the bug was reported on. It serves the docs site built on Linux by the workflow's docs-site job (E2E_PREBUILT=1): the site does not build on Windows (bake-newcomer-frame: `module is not defined` in lib/core/content-policy.js, run 44853144110; followups.d/3345-p3-docs-build-on-windows.md).
